doc.title: Tokens
doc.para: Tokens During interpretation, scripts are completely broken down into units called tokens and processed. The boundary between one token and the next varies depending on the token type.

Bare Words "Bare words" refer to specific sequences of characters written directly in the script without being quoted with "" or ''. "Bare words" follow these rules:
Composed of lowercase and uppercase alphabetic characters, '_' (underscore), digits, and so-called full-width characters. However, digits cannot come at the beginning.
The sequence until its end is treated as a single "bare word".
ampan // OK 123a // NG because a digit comes first _asdf // OK because underscores can be at the beginning continue // This is a reserved word OK 全角文字 // So-called full-width characters are OK as "bare words"
"Bare words" are further classified into reserved words and identifiers.

Reserved Words Reserved words are as follows and are not identifiers. Any "bare word" that is not a reserved word is an identifier.
break continue const catch class case debugger default delete do extends export enum else function finally false for global getter goto incontextof Infinity invalidate instanceof isvalid import int in if NaN null new octet protected property private public return real synchronized switch static setter string super typeof throw this true try void var while with
These reserved words each have special meanings for important uses in constructing the script syntax. Some of these are used as operators. However, not all of these reserved words are used in the current version.

Identifiers "Identifiers" are all "bare words" that are not reserved words. These are used for variables, functions, class names, etc., that the writer can freely name. Even if an identifier contains a reserved word, as long as it is not the reserved word itself, it will be recognized as an identifier rather than a reserved word.

Symbols Symbols are also broken down as tokens. Symbols include the following:
>>>= >>> >>= >> >= > <<= <= <-> << < === == => = !== != ! &&= && &= & ||= || |= | ... . ++ += + -= -- - *= * /= / \= \ %= % ^= ^ [ ] ( ) ~ ? : , ; { } # $
These are extracted as tokens using greedy matching (longest match). For example, ++ is broken down as a single symbol ++, not as + and +. If you want to write them as separate + and +, you need to insert a space or similar between + and +.
Symbols each have an important meaning as elements constructing the syntax. Some symbols are used as operators.

Numeric Literals Numeric literals begin with a digit or . (decimal point). TJS2 recognizes the following formats: Writing numbers normally yields decimal numeric literals.
0 3.1 342.3 1
Also, for decimal numbers, you can specify a base-10 exponent using e or E. Both e and E have the same meaning.
1e-3 // 1×10-3 3.4e10 // 3.4×1010 9.3E-2 // 9.3×10-2
Prefixing with 0x or 0X specifies a hexadecimal number. Both 0x and 0X have the same meaning.
0x1234 0Xff 0x3f33
Prefixing with 0b or 0B specifies a binary number.
0b0100 0B0010100010100001
Prefixing with 0 treats it as an octal number.
01234 033
Decimal point formats and base-2 exponent specification using p are also possible for hexadecimal, octal, and binary. p specifies an exponent with base 2.
0b1.1 // Represents 1.5 as 1 + 1/2 0x2.f // Represents 2.9375 as 2 + 15/16 0x1p8 // Represents 256.0 as 1 × 28
Numeric literals are treated as a single numeric literal as long as the characters are valid components of a numeric literal.

String Literals String literals are enclosed in "" (double quotation marks) or '' (single quotation marks). You may use either double quotation marks or single quotation marks. However, inside "" (double quotation marks), you do not need to escape ' (single quotation mark) with \, and inside '' (single quotation marks), you do not need to escape " (double quotation mark).
"this is a string." 'this is also a string.' "Can't use without a quotation."
Inside a string, \ (backslash / yen sign) has a special meaning. The meaning changes depending on the character that follows \. Making a special specification after \ is called escaping.
\\ : The \ mark itself \' : ' (single quotation mark) \" : " (double quotation mark) \a : BEL (audible bell) \b : BS (backspace) \f : FF (form feed) \n : LF (line feed) \r : CR (carriage return)
\t : HT (horizontal tab) \v : VT (vertical tab) \xH : H=hexadecimal number (H represents the character code) \XH : Same as above
In the \xH format, specify a hexadecimal number for the H portion. That hexadecimal number will then be treated as a character code and replaced with that single character.
'Can\'t help' ( using \' ) "\x1234" ( character with character code 0x1234 as a wide character )
Also, in the \xH format, as long as valid hexadecimal characters (0–9, A–F, a–f) follow \x, they are considered part of H. However, up to 4 digits are recognized in environments where the wide character size is 16-bit, and up to 8 digits on 32-bit machines (16-bit for Windows, 32-bit for Linux or Solaris). Writing "\x22An Apple" causes the beginning to be treated as \x22A. To avoid this, separate the strings and write them consecutively as "\x22" "An Apple". In TJS, when string literals are consecutive like this, they are treated as a single string.
Please also refer to regarding strings.

String Literals with @ Placing @ before a string literal causes the content between & and ; or between ${ and } in that string literal to be treated as an expression, and the result of evaluating it will be expanded there (writing an expression between & and ; or between ${ and } embeds its result there). If you do not want to expand & or $, you can prevent expansion by placing \ before & or $.
@"1+2=&1+2;" ( becomes the string "1+2=3" ) @"The content of variable f is &f;" ( expands the content of variable f at the position of &f; ) @"The result of calling function func is &func();" ( any valid expression can be written between & and ; ) @"The result of calling function func is ${func()}" ( same as above ) @"true \&\& false is &true && false;" ( writing \ before & prevents & from being expanded )
Expressions written here can access variables and other entities (including local variables) that are accessible from where this string is written.

Octet Sequence Literals Octet sequence literals are enclosed in <% and %>, inside of which octet data (binary data) can be written. Multiple data entries are specified as two-digit hexadecimal numbers separated by spaces or other whitespace.
<% 00 01 02 03 %> <% ff ff ff 00 04 0f ff 30 %>
Please also refer to regarding octet sequences.

Regular Expression Patterns Regular expression patterns are enclosed in / and /, inside of which regular expression patterns can be written. Flag characters can be written following the regular expression pattern: g is the global search flag (matches all occurrences; without this flag, it matches only the first one), i is the case-insensitive flag for alphabetic characters, and l is the flag to perform localized collation. Regular expression patterns written in this manner are treated as objects of the RegExp class.
/[0-9]-[0-9]-[0-9]/ /^;\s*(.*?)\s*=(.*)$/ /start(.*?)end/gi
Please also refer to regarding regular expression patterns.
